questions.stem: Why was the area around Pompeii and Herculaneum attractive for settlement and farming?
options: Fertile volcanic soils, a mild climate and access to the Bay of Naples
Rich deposits of gold and silver mined from the upper slopes of Vesuvius
Its distance from the sea, which protected it from pirate attacks
Heavy summer rainfall that made irrigation of crops unnecessary
questions.explanation: Weathered volcanic soils made Campania highly productive for vines, olives and grain, and the bay gave access to sea trade. Pompeii also lay near the mouth of the Sarno River, which linked it to the inland towns.

questions.stem: The Greek geographer Strabo, writing before 79 CE, described the summit of Vesuvius as barren and ash-coloured, with rocks that looked burnt. What does this suggest?
options: Some observers saw signs of past volcanic activity, though it was not known to be active
Romans expected an eruption and had already evacuated the towns around the mountain
Vesuvius had erupted many times during the lifetime of Strabo and of his own readers
The mountain had been deliberately burnt by farmers to clear land for vineyards
questions.explanation: Strabo inferred from the summit's appearance that it had once been on fire, but there was no recorded eruption in Roman memory. The towns were therefore not prepared for what happened in 79 CE.

questions.stem: A strong earthquake struck Pompeii and Herculaneum in 62 CE (Seneca dates it to 63). Why is it important for interpreting the evidence from 79 CE?
options: It destroyed both towns completely, and they were never reoccupied after it
It caused the first recorded eruption, which buried part of Herculaneum
It led the emperor to move the population of Pompeii to Naples for good
Many buildings were still damaged or under repair when the eruption came
questions.explanation: Evidence of repair work, such as the rebuilt Temple of Isis and the unfinished Central Baths, shows the towns were still recovering. The remains of 79 CE are therefore not a picture of a 'normal' Roman town.

questions.stem: Which written source gives the only surviving eyewitness account of the eruption of 79 CE?
options: The Roman History of Cassius Dio, written at the time
Two letters of Pliny the Younger to the historian Tacitus
The Annals of Tacitus, written from his own observation
The Natural History of Pliny the Elder, finished at Stabiae
questions.explanation: Pliny the Younger watched the eruption from Misenum and described it, and his uncle's death, in two letters written about 25 years later. Pliny the Elder died during the eruption, and Cassius Dio wrote more than a century afterwards.

questions.stem: In the first phase of the eruption, Pompeii, lying south-east of Vesuvius, was mainly affected by:
options: a lava flow that ran slowly through the streets and set the buildings alight
a tsunami from the bay that swept away the houses near the forum
a mudflow of boiling water that filled every building to the rooftops
a heavy fall of pumice and ash carried by the wind, which collapsed roofs
questions.explanation: The wind carried the eruption column's pumice and ash over Pompeii for many hours, and the weight brought down roofs. Pyroclastic surges and flows came later. Lava did not reach the towns.

questions.stem: Why are organic materials such as wooden furniture, food and papyrus scrolls far better preserved at Herculaneum than at Pompeii?
options: Herculaneum was covered only by a thin layer of ash that later blew away
Herculaneum was buried deep under hot pyroclastic deposits that carbonised them
Herculaneum was abandoned well before the eruption, so nothing there was disturbed
Herculaneum lay under the sea for centuries, which kept out the oxygen
questions.explanation: Pyroclastic flows buried Herculaneum under a far deeper layer of material that hardened into rock, carbonising wood, food and scrolls and sealing them in. At Pompeii much organic material decayed in the looser pumice and ash.

questions.stem: Pliny the Younger dates the eruption to the ninth day before the Kalends of September (24 August). Many scholars now favour a date in autumn 79 CE. Which evidence supports their view?
options: Inscriptions recording elections that were held in Pompeii in December
A charcoal inscription dated to mid-October, and remains of autumn fruits
A coin of Augustus found in a victim's purse at Herculaneum's boat sheds
Tacitus' Annals, which give the eruption's exact day and the weather that day
questions.explanation: Finds such as pomegranates, heavier clothing, braziers and a charcoal inscription dated to mid-October, uncovered in 2018, suggest a later date. The manuscripts of Pliny's letter also vary, so the date remains debated.

questions.stem: From the 1980s, hundreds of skeletons were found in the vaulted boat sheds on Herculaneum's ancient shoreline. How did this discovery change interpretations?
options: It overturned the earlier view that nearly all Herculaneum's people had escaped
It proved that Herculaneum had been abandoned years before the eruption began
It showed that all of the victims were enslaved people left behind by their owners
It confirmed that the pyroclastic flows had never reached Herculaneum at all
questions.explanation: Very few bodies had been found in the town, so it was long assumed most residents fled. The boat-shed skeletons of men, women and children, studied by Sara Bisel and others, showed many had sought refuge on the shore.

questions.stem: Painted notices on Pompeii's walls urging people to vote for particular candidates are called:
options: lararia
fasces
tabernae (shops)
programmata
questions.explanation: Programmata were painted electoral notices, often naming the supporters, such as a trade group or neighbours. Lararia were household shrines and tabernae were shops.

questions.stem: Giuseppe Fiorelli's technique of 1863 produced the famous casts of Pompeii's victims by:
options: pouring plaster into cavities in the ash left by bodies that had decomposed
covering the skeletons found lying in the streets with a layer of wet plaster
carving copies of the victims from photographs taken during excavation
filling the boat sheds at Herculaneum with plaster to protect the bones
questions.explanation: Bodies decayed inside the hardened ash, leaving hollows in their shape; plaster poured in captured posture and clothing. The casts contain the victims' bones, which raises ethical questions about their display.

questions.stem: A student argues that Pompeii is a city 'frozen in time' that shows a normal day of Roman life. Which is the strongest objection to this argument?
options: No objects at all were found in the houses because the eruption destroyed everything
Pompeii was not a Roman town in 79 CE but an independent Greek city that kept its own laws
The plaster casts show that every resident died in their homes during the first hour
Many residents fled and took valuables, and the town was still repairing earthquake damage
questions.explanation: Historians such as Mary Beard stress that the remains reflect a town in crisis: people fled carrying valuables, buildings were damaged, and later salvage and looting disturbed the site. Pompeii had been a Roman colony since 80 BCE.

questions.stem: Graffiti scratched into Pompeii's walls are valuable to historians mainly because they:
options: record the words of a wider range of people than formal literature does
give a complete and unbiased record of the opinions of every resident
were written by the town council as official records of its decisions
were all written by visiting Greek scholars describing the town for Rome
questions.explanation: Graffiti include greetings, jokes, prices, insults and messages from people who never wrote literature. They are still biased towards the literate and to particular places, so they are not complete.

questions.stem: Tacitus records a riot at Pompeii's amphitheatre in 59 CE between Pompeians and people from Nuceria, after which the Senate banned games at Pompeii for ten years. A fresco found in a Pompeian house shows fighting in and around the amphitheatre. Together these sources:
options: prove the fresco was painted in Rome and later carried to the town
show that the riot happened in Herculaneum rather than in Pompeii
corroborate each other, as a written and a visual source of the same event
contradict each other, since Tacitus claims the amphitheatre was never used
questions.explanation: The Roman historian's account and a local painting independently record the same riot, which strengthens the evidence. A historian would still note Tacitus wrote decades later and the fresco's purpose is uncertain.

questions.stem: Which is the most significant limitation of the early excavations at Pompeii and Herculaneum in the 18th century as a source for historians today?
options: Every find was reburied, so nothing from those excavations has survived at all
Objects and frescoes were removed with little record of where they were found
The excavators used modern scientific dating that has since proved to be wrong
The excavators published too many detailed site plans for historians to read
questions.explanation: Bourbon-era diggers tunnelled for treasure and cut paintings from walls for the royal collection, now largely in the Naples National Archaeological Museum. Without find-spots, objects lose much of their context.

questions.stem: The Temple of Isis was rebuilt after the earthquake in the name of a six-year-old boy, Numerius Popidius Celsinus, who was then admitted to the town council. Historians usually explain this as:
options: proof that the emperor appointed every member of Pompeii's town council
a freedman father, barred from office himself, advancing his freeborn son
a sign that Pompeii allowed young children to be elected as senior magistrates
evidence that the cult of Isis was banned and had to be revived in secret
questions.explanation: His father, Numerius Popidius Ampliatus, was a freedman and so could not hold office, but his son was freeborn. Funding the rebuilding won the family status. The inscription shows both the wealth and the limits facing freedmen.

questions.stem: Eumachia is a significant figure for the study of women in Pompeii because she:
options: wrote a history of Pompeii that survives as a complete literary text
was a public priestess who paid for a large building on the forum
was elected as one of the two duoviri, the town's chief magistrates
led the town's defence and organised the evacuation during the eruption
questions.explanation: Eumachia, a public priestess, built a large building on the forum, and the fullers dedicated a statue to her. Women could not vote or hold office, but wealthy women could gain public status through priesthoods and patronage.

questions.stem: An inscription advertised the lease of baths, shops and upper-floor rooms on the property of Julia Felix in Pompeii. It is evidence that:
options: women were the only people allowed to own the public baths
Julia Felix was a magistrate who controlled the town's markets
all properties in Pompeii were owned by the town council
some women owned property and managed it as a business
questions.explanation: Julia Felix leased parts of her large property, showing a woman acting as an owner and landlord. Women could own and manage property, though they were excluded from political office.

questions.stem: Wax tablets from Herculaneum record a lawsuit in which a woman, Petronia Justa, claimed she was born free after her mother was freed, while another woman claimed she was born a slave. This source is valuable mainly because it shows:
options: how important, and how disputed, legal status could be in daily life
that enslaved people in Herculaneum could never be legally freed
that women were not permitted to bring their cases before Roman courts
that everyone in Herculaneum kept written proof of their birth
questions.explanation: The case turned on whether she was born before or after her mother's manumission, which decided whether she was freeborn. It shows that freedom could be granted, that women went to law, and that status was hard to prove.

questions.stem: The two senior annually elected magistrates of Pompeii, who presided over the town council and the courts, were the:
options: tribunes
duoviri
aediles
consuls
questions.explanation: The duoviri (duumviri) were the chief magistrates, while the two aediles looked after streets, markets, public buildings and games. Consuls and tribunes were magistrates of Rome itself.

questions.stem: A historian uses Pompeii's election notices to argue that most Pompeians took an active part in local politics. Which is the main problem with this argument?
options: The notices were painted after the eruption by the excavators to attract more visitors to the site
The notices show that elections were abolished in Pompeii when it became a Roman colony
The notices were written in Greek, so few people in Pompeii could have read any of them
The notices name supporters who could not vote, such as women, and favour wealthy candidates
questions.explanation: Some notices were put up in the names of women, who could not vote, and only wealthy freeborn men could stand. The notices show public interest in elections but not how widely or freely people voted.

questions.stem: Aulus Umbricius Scaurus of Pompeii, whose house had a floor mosaic showing labelled jars of his product, made his fortune producing:
options: wine from the slopes of Vesuvius
woollen cloth for the army
olive oil for the lamps of Rome
garum, a fermented fish sauce
questions.explanation: Scaurus was a leading producer of garum, and his containers have been found beyond Pompeii. The mosaic shows how an owner advertised the source of his family's wealth.

questions.stem: Fulleries (fullonicae) such as the one of Stephanus in Pompeii were businesses that:
options: sold hot food and drink from counters facing the street
minted coins for the town council and the local markets
cleaned and finished cloth, using treading vats and urine
baked bread in large brick ovens with mills turned by donkeys
questions.explanation: Fullers trod garments in vats with urine and other substances to clean and finish wool. Bakeries had mills and ovens, and thermopolia were street-front food counters.

questions.stem: In a Roman house (domus), the impluvium was:
options: a small shrine to the household gods in the corner of the kitchen
the dining room where guests reclined on couches around a table
the main room at the back where the owner received his clients
a shallow pool in the atrium collecting rain from the roof opening
questions.explanation: Rain fell through the compluvium, the opening in the atrium roof, into the impluvium and drained to a cistern. The household shrine was the lararium, the dining room the triclinium and the reception room the tablinum.

questions.stem: Andrew Wallace-Hadrill argued that Roman houses in Pompeii and Herculaneum were not 'private' in the modern sense. Which evidence best supports this view?
options: Every house had a separate kitchen building, located well away from all of the main living rooms
Most houses had no doors, so people could walk freely through every room at any time
Owners lived in villas outside the town and visited their town houses only for festivals
Clients visited the atrium each morning, and views through the house displayed the owner's status
questions.explanation: In the morning salutatio clients came to the atrium, and lines of sight from the entrance through to the tablinum and garden displayed the owner's wealth. Houses mixed family life with public business, shops and work.

questions.stem: Why does Herculaneum provide better evidence than Pompeii for the upper storeys of houses and for wooden fittings?
options: The deep, hot deposits preserved upper floors and carbonised wood in place
Herculaneum's houses were built of marble rather than of timber and brick
Herculaneum's houses were excavated in the 18th century using modern methods
Herculaneum's houses were rebuilt by Maiuri using their original timbers
questions.explanation: At Herculaneum upper floors, balconies, and fittings such as the carbonised folding partition in the House of the Wooden Partition survive. At Pompeii most roofs and upper floors collapsed under the weight of pumice.

questions.stem: Pompeii's amphitheatre, built about 70 BCE, is significant because it:
options: was used only for plays and concerts, never for gladiatorial shows
is the earliest surviving stone amphitheatre in the Roman world
is the largest amphitheatre ever built, larger than Rome's Colosseum
was built only after the earthquake to replace a theatre that collapsed
questions.explanation: Built by two local magistrates soon after the colony was founded, it is the oldest surviving stone amphitheatre. It hosted gladiatorial games, which were advertised in painted notices around the town.

questions.stem: In the public baths of Pompeii and Herculaneum, the caldarium was the:
options: open exercise yard surrounded by columns
hot room, heated by a hypocaust under the floor
cold plunge pool used at the very end of a visit
changing room with niches for clothing
questions.explanation: Bathers moved between the apodyterium (changing room), frigidarium (cold), tepidarium (warm) and caldarium (hot), which was heated by hot air under the floors and in the walls. The exercise yard was the palaestra.

questions.stem: Pompeii's water supply in 79 CE came mainly from:
options: an aqueduct feeding a distribution tower near the Vesuvius Gate
the Sarno River, pumped uphill to every house by enslaved workers
seawater from the bay, purified in large tanks inside the forum
underground springs that rose directly beneath the Temple of Apollo
questions.explanation: A branch of the Aqua Augusta aqueduct reached the castellum aquae near the Vesuvius Gate, where lead pipes carried water to fountains, baths and some houses. Wells and rainwater cisterns remained important too.

questions.stem: Analysis of material from a drain beneath one of Herculaneum's streets found remains of fish, sea urchin, fruits, nuts and seeds. What can a historian most reasonably conclude?
options: The ordinary residents who used it ate a varied diet including seafood
Every resident of Herculaneum ate exactly the same diet each day
Seafood was eaten only by the elite and never by any ordinary people
The drain shows that Herculaneum had no public latrines at all
questions.explanation: The waste came from the households above the drain, many of them modest, so it gives direct evidence of everyday diet. It cannot show what every person ate, and other evidence suggests diets varied by sex and status.

questions.stem: Pompeii's high stepping stones across the streets are evidence that:
options: streets also carried rainwater and waste, so walkers crossed above them
carts were banned from the town and the streets were used only by people
the streets were flooded by the sea every day at high tide
pedestrians had to pay a toll to cross the street at each stepping stone
questions.explanation: Pompeii had limited sewers, so water from fountains and rain, along with waste, ran along the streets. Gaps between the stones let cart wheels pass, as wheel ruts show.

questions.stem: A lararium found in many houses in Pompeii and Herculaneum was:
options: a public temple to Jupiter, Juno and Minerva in the forum
a building where the priests of the emperor met and dined together
a burial chamber for family members outside the town walls
a household shrine to the Lares and the genius of the family
questions.explanation: Families made daily offerings at the lararium, which often showed the Lares, the genius of the head of the household and snakes. Public religion centred on temples such as the Capitolium in the forum.

questions.stem: The Temple of Isis at Pompeii shows that:
options: Egyptian priests ruled Pompeii in place of its elected Roman magistrates
the cult of Isis was banned in Pompeii and practised only in private homes
cults from the eastern Mediterranean had followers alongside traditional Roman gods
worship of the traditional Roman gods had ended in Pompeii well before the year 79 CE
questions.explanation: Isis, an Egyptian goddess, offered personal salvation through initiation, and her temple was rebuilt after the earthquake. It stood alongside temples of Jupiter, Apollo and Venus, the colony's patron goddess.

questions.stem: Amedeo Maiuri, director of excavations from 1924 to 1961, is known for:
options: first identifying Pompeii by name from an inscription found in 1763
open-area excavation of Herculaneum and large clearances at Pompeii
tunnelling into Herculaneum to find statues for the Bourbon king
inventing the plaster cast method later used for the victims of Pompeii
questions.explanation: Maiuri uncovered much of Herculaneum in the open from 1927 and excavated widely at Pompeii, including along the Via dell'Abbondanza. Some of his restorations used reinforced concrete, which later caused conservation problems.

questions.stem: In 2010 the Schola Armaturarum (House of the Gladiators) in Pompeii collapsed after heavy rain. This event led most directly to:
options: the EU-funded Great Pompeii Project to stabilise and conserve the site
the immediate closure of Pompeii to all visitors for the following decade
a decision to rebury all of Pompeii to protect it from further damage
a new program of excavation to uncover the rest of Herculaneum quickly
questions.explanation: The collapse drew international criticism, and the Great Pompeii Project began in 2012 with European Union funding for conservation, drainage and site management. The focus shifted towards protecting what was already exposed.

questions.stem: Since 2001 the Herculaneum Conservation Project has focused mainly on:
options: removing all frescoes from the walls and sending them to foreign museums
rebuilding the town's houses with new materials for tourist visits
conserving the exposed site, including drainage, roofing and maintenance
excavating the whole of the modern town of Ercolano above the ancient one
questions.explanation: The project, a partnership involving the Packard Humanities Institute and the Italian heritage authorities, prioritised drainage, protective roofing and regular maintenance over new excavation. Much of the ancient town remains under modern Ercolano.

questions.stem: DNA analysis of victims inside several Pompeii plaster casts, published in 2024, found that an adult long described as a mother holding a child was a man unrelated to the child. What does this show about interpretation?
options: Earlier stories about the victims often projected modern assumptions onto them
The plaster casts are modern fakes containing no human remains at all
DNA analysis proves that the Pompeii victims all died before the eruption began
Fiorelli's casts were made only of animals that had died in the eruption
questions.explanation: Relationships had been inferred from position and appearance, shaped by modern ideas about family and gender. Scientific testing of the remains showed several such stories were wrong, a reminder to test interpretations against evidence.

questions.stem: Carbonised papyrus scrolls from the Villa of the Papyri at Herculaneum cannot be unrolled without damage. How have researchers begun to read them?
options: by X-ray scanning the scrolls and using computer methods to reveal the ink
by soaking the scrolls in warm water until the layers separate on their own
by comparing them with complete copies held in the library at Alexandria
by heating the scrolls again until the ink becomes visible on the surface
questions.explanation: High-resolution X-ray scans and machine learning have revealed Greek text inside unopened scrolls, much of it Epicurean philosophy. Earlier attempts to unroll scrolls by hand destroyed many of them.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states an ethical issue raised by the display of the Pompeii plaster casts?
options: The casts are too fragile to be studied scientifically by any modern method
The casts were made illegally by tourists without the permission of Italy
The casts show victims whose names and families are all fully recorded
The casts contain human remains, yet are shown to the public as a spectacle
questions.explanation: Because the casts contain bones, displaying and touring them raises questions of dignity and respect for people who cannot consent. Against this, many argue they help visitors connect with the human cost of the eruption.

questions.stem: Which is a negative impact of mass tourism on Pompeii?
options: the complete loss of all government funding for conservation work at the site
the flooding of the site by the sea because of the visitors' boats
the reburial of most of the town to keep the visitors away from it
wear on paving and floors, crowding, graffiti and the theft of small items
questions.explanation: Millions of visitors wear down surfaces and some damage or steal material, but ticket income also funds conservation. Managing visitor numbers while keeping the site open is a continuing challenge.

questions.stem: Edward Bulwer-Lytton's novel The Last Days of Pompeii (1834) and many later films portray the town as luxurious and doomed. How should a historian treat such representations?
options: As evidence of later attitudes to Pompeii, not as evidence of life there in 79 CE
As reliable sources for daily life, since the authors had all visited the site in person
As eyewitness accounts that are more accurate than the archaeological evidence
As official histories produced by the Italian authorities for school students
questions.explanation: Popular representations reflect the concerns and tastes of their own times, such as moral lessons about luxury and spectacular death. They can shape public views of the site, so historians study them critically against the evidence.
